h1:
Hua Hin Night Market
An after-dark eating crawl
intro: Once the sky goes dark, Hua Hin Soi 72 turns into a long lane of food. Charcoal smoke from grilling prawns and squid, pad thai sizzling in hot woks, and the bright lights of the stalls — this is the dinner almost everyone who comes to Hua Hin ends up stopping for. We walk it from the top of the lane to the far end, picking out the stalls that are worth your money, with honest prices along the way.

blocks.html: Hua Hin Night Market runs along Soi Hua Hin 72, off Phetkasem Road, and you can walk to it from the town centre and Hua Hin Beach. It's open every day from around 6pm until midnight — an old, long-running night food market with hundreds of stalls, from pick-your-own seafood to old-school dessert vendors. If it's your first time, walk the full length of the lane before you commit to anything, because the good stuff is spread across both sides.

The star of this market is the seafood stalls that lay out prawns, shellfish, squid and crab on beds of ice out front. You walk up, point at what you want, pay by weight or by the piece, and they grill or cook it fresh. Prices swing with size and season, so ask before you order every time and you'll save yourself the surprise at the till.

items.name: Pa Jaeng Fresh & Dried Squid
items.blurb: The go-to grilled squid stall in the market. Big squid grilled over charcoal until fragrant, dipped in punchy seafood sauce, with oyster omelette on the side too. There's almost always a small queue here.

items.name: Pick-your-own seafood stalls at the lane entrance (KO / Duangjai)
items.blurb: A cluster of seafood stalls with trays of prawns, shellfish and squid out front to choose from. Order grilled prawns, grilled squid or blanched shellfish however you like — cooked fresh right in front of you. Great if you come as a group and share.
items.meta: Pick fresh, grilled/steamed · pay by weight

items.name: Je Tim Fish Rice Soup
items.blurb: If you want something warm and a hot bowl of broth, this stall does fish rice soup and seafood tom yum — bold, well-balanced flavours. Good to finish a meal or for a cooler evening.

blocks.title: Seafood tip
blocks.html: Most pick-your-own stalls charge by weight. Before they put it on the scale, ask the price per kilo and keep an eye on the scale too, so the final bill doesn't catch you off guard. Seafood that looks fresh — clear eyes, firm flesh — is a good sign.

blocks.text: Pad thai, oyster omelette and hot savoury plates

blocks.html: There's no shortage of hot plates here: pad thai from a steel wok with that wood-fire aroma, crispy oyster omelette, pork satay, grilled pork skewers, all the way to fried chicken. Easy to eat as you walk.

items.name: Pad Thai Mae Yai
items.blurb: Pad thai from a hot wok with chewy, tender noodles and a well-balanced flavour that leans slightly sweet. Order it with prawns or wrapped in egg. The same stall does oyster omelette and pork satay if you want to add on.
items.meta: Pad thai · oyster omelette · pork satay

items.name: Lung Tae Grilled Pork Skewers
items.blurb: An old-school pork-skewer stall in the middle of the lane that's been going for decades. Sweet, fragrant marinated pork grilled over charcoal, eaten with hot sticky rice — an easy-to-find snack while you walk that Thais love.

items.name: Old-school Hua Hin Fried Chicken
items.blurb: Crispy-skinned, juicy fried chicken, made fresh and hot — good as a side dish or a snack while you walk. A stall the regulars know well.

items.name: Hua Hin Meatballs
items.blurb: Grilled pork meatballs and noodles — easy, light, cheap filler. Good to break up a meal before moving on to the next stall.

blocks.html: Once you've eaten your fill of savoury stuff, the dessert side is still waiting — from old-school ice cream and mango sticky rice to crepes and cold Thai sweets in a cup.

items.name: Ni Ice Cream @Hua Hin
items.blurb: A well-loved ice cream stall in the market with 6–7 flavours to choose from, around ฿30. Customers come and go all day — an easy dessert to finish on.

items.name: Than Khun Mango Sticky Rice
items.blurb: Soft coconut-soaked sticky rice with sweet ripe mango — the classic Thai dessert that foreign visitors fall for too.

items.name: Mae Tap Thai Sweets
items.blurb: Cold tao tueng and mixed Thai sweets in a cup, around ฿30 — good for cooling off after a long walk around the market.

items.name: 72 Crepes
items.blurb: Crispy crepes in lots of flavours, around ฿50, both savoury and sweet, made fresh in front of you.

blocks.title: Tips for making the most of the market
blocks.html: Start at the top of Soi 72 and walk all the way to the end first, then double back on the other side, so you've seen everything before deciding. If you still want more, head over to nearby Soi Dechanuchit, which has even more food stalls. Bring enough cash, because many stalls take cash only.

items: Opening hours — daily, roughly 6pm to midnight; it gets busy after about 7pm.
Parking — park near Wat Hua Hin or along the streets close to the market, for a small fee; spots fill up fast in high season.
Getting there — off Phetkasem Road via Soi Hua Hin 72; walkable from stays in the town centre and by the beach.
Cash — keep small notes handy; most stalls take cash, with prices from tens to hundreds of baht.

faq.q: Where is Hua Hin Night Market and what time does it open?
faq.a: It's on Soi Hua Hin 72, off Phetkasem Road, and walkable from the town centre and Hua Hin Beach. It's open every day from around 6pm until midnight, and gets busy from about 7pm onwards.

faq.q: What's good to eat at Hua Hin Night Market?
faq.a: The star is pick-your-own seafood — grilled prawns, grilled squid and oyster omelette — followed by hot plates like pad thai, Lung Tae's grilled pork skewers and fried chicken, plus old-school desserts like Ni ice cream, mango sticky rice and cold tao tueng.

faq.q: Is seafood at the market expensive, and how is it priced?
faq.a: Most pick-your-own stalls charge by weight, and prices swing with size and season. Before you order, ask the price per kilo and watch the scale. Snacks like pork skewers, meatballs and pad thai start from tens up to a few hundred baht, which is light on the wallet.

faq.q: Does Hua Hin Night Market take cards, and how much cash should I bring?
faq.a: Most stalls take cash only, so bring small notes. A dinner of grazing across a few stalls runs roughly 150–400 baht per person and leaves you full; add more if you order big shared seafood plates, depending on how many of you there are.

faq.q: Are there other markets near Hua Hin Night Market to carry on to?
faq.a: Yes — if you still want more, walk over to nearby Soi Dechanuchit, which has extra food stalls. Other popular night markets in Hua Hin include Cicada Market and Tamarind Market, which only open on certain days.
